extracted.intended_audience: professional mathematicians and mathematical researchers (geometers, number theorists, analysts, algebraists, topologists)
extracted.subtask_description: A numbered list of posed research problems across multiple mathematical fields (geometry, group theory, analysis, number theory, algebra, topology), each giving a precise open question, context, and suggested directions or methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lie's concept of a continuous group of transformations without the assumption of the differentiability of the functions defining the group
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether Lie's theory of continuous groups of transformations can be developed without assuming differentiability of the defining functions; in particular, determine whether differentiability is an independent postulate or can be derived from the group concept together with other axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study reduction to analytic (differentiable) groups via introduction of new variables/parameters; note Schur's theorem that reduction to analytic groups is possible for transitive groups assuming existence of first and certain second derivatives. Explore infinite groups, functional equations usually treated with differentiability (Abel-type, difference equations), and the question of proving differentiability from existence of difference equations. Examples: Minkowski's convexity-related functional equation leading to differential quotients; constructions of analytic functional equations whose only solutions are non-differentiable (via trigonometric series or Borel/Picard-style constructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical treatment of the axioms of physics
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate and treat physical theories (notably probability theory and mechanics) axiomatically in the same rigorous fashion used for geometry; include development of mean-value methods in mathematical physics and kinetic theory of gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematicians should develop limiting processes (e.g., from atomistic models to continuum laws of motion), test compatibility of new axioms with existing ones, and survey all logically possible theories. Draw on works of Mach, Hertz, Boltzmann, Volkmann; aim for exact formulations and proofs of compatibility rather than relying on experimental intuition. Lie's principle of subdivision and infinite transformation groups may inform subdivisions of physical axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrationality and transcendence of certain numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend results of Hermite and Lindemann: investigate when special transcendental functions take algebraic or transcendental values at algebraic arguments; prove statements such as certain expressions with algebraic bases and irrational algebraic exponents are transcendental or at least irrational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and conjectures: geometric formulation (in an isosceles triangle with algebraic but nonrational ratio of angles, the ratio base/side is transcendental); expect new methods will be required. Study classes of transcendental functions important in analysis and whether they assume transcendental values for algebraic (irrational) arguments. Work should lead to new insights about special irrational and transcendental numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems of prime numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Advance the understanding of the distribution of prime numbers, in particular by addressing Riemann's conjecture that nontrivial zeros of the zeta function have real part 1/2, refine Riemann's prime-counting formula, and investigate related problems such as Goldbach's conjecture and twin primes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build on results of Hadamard, de la Vallée-Poussin, von Mangoldt. After resolving the zero-distribution (Riemann hypothesis), test the accuracy of Riemann's series for the number of primes ≤ x and whether the error term has order not greater than x^{1/2}. Study whether observed local condensations of primes are due to contributions of first complex zeros. Further goals: attempt rigorous solutions of Goldbach's problem and twin-prime questions, and general linear Diophantine equations in primes. Extend techniques to distribution of ideal primes in number fields via ζ_k(s) = ∑ N(j)^{-s}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of the most general law of reciprocity in any number field
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove the reciprocity law for residues of l-th powers in any number field, for odd prime l and for l equal to powers of 2 or of an odd prime; generalize reciprocity to arbitrary algebraic realms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect the law and methods to arise by generalizing the theory of l-th roots of unity and Hilbert's theory of relative quadratic fields. The result will likely connect to class field theory and the arithmetic foundations developed by Hilbert and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of the solvability of a diophantine equation
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a Diophantine equation with any number of unknowns and integer coefficients, devise a finite procedure (a process of a finite number of operations) to decide whether the equation has an integer solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate a decision procedure for solvability in integers. (This is an explicit finiteness/decidability problem for integral solutions of arbitrary polynomial equations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadratic forms with any algebraic numerical coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop the theory of quadratic forms in any number of variables with arbitrary algebraic coefficients; in particular, determine solvability of such quadratic equations in integers or fractions from the algebraic realm determined by the coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use knowledge from the theory of quadratic number fields to attack general quadratic forms. The aim includes solving given quadratic equations with algebraic coefficients by integral or fractional numbers within the corresponding field of rationality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of Kronecker's theorem on abelian fields to any algebraic realm of rationality
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend Kronecker's theorem (that every abelian number field arises from Q by adjoining roots of unity) to imaginary quadratic fields (via elliptic functions) and ultimately to arbitrary algebraic fields of rationality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two parts of Kronecker's theorem (existence/count of equations with given group/discriminant, and representation via transcendental functions like e^{2πi z}) suggest analogous function-theoretic constructions (exponential for Q, elliptic modular functions for imaginary quadratic fields). Use complex multiplication, Weber's theory, and class-field theory. The general law of reciprocity for residues of l-th powers is a key arithmetical ingredient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility of the solution of the general equation of the 7-th degree by means of functions of only two arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish that the root of the general 7th-degree equation cannot be expressed by a finite composition (chain) of continuous functions each depending on only two arguments (the nomographic class).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nomography constructs multivariable functions by iterated two-argument functions; show that the 7th-degree root cannot be so constructed (i.e., not a function obtainable by a finite number of insertions of functions of two arguments). Hilbert notes he has shown existence of analytical functions of three variables not obtainable by such finite chains. Tschirnhausen transformations reduce degrees for 5th and 6th, explaining solvability there. Movable elements in nomography (d'Ocagne) can extend constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of the finiteness of certain complete systems of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: In invariant theory and related areas, decide whether the set of relatively integral functions (those that become integral after a specified substitution) always forms a finite field of integrality—i.e., whether a finite subset can generate all others rationally and integrally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate using the notion of a finite field of integrality: choose a finite number of functions from which all others of the system are rationally and integrally expressible. Consider refined number-theoretic versions where coefficients are integers and expressions involve powers of a prime p (G(X_1,...,X_m)·X_1^{h1}...X_m^{hm} with exponents h). Use elimination theory, Kronecker's algebraic modular systems, and results by Gordan, Hilbert, Maurer, Hurwitz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous foundation of Schubert's enumerative calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a rigorous justification and precise determination of the scope/limits for the enumerative numbers Schubert obtained using the principle of special position (conservation of number) in enumerative geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although algebraic elimination theory in principle allows carrying out the necessary calculations, one must actually perform elimination for equations of special form so that the degree of final equations and multiplicities of solutions are predictable. Establish exact conditions under which Schubert's counts are valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem of the topology of algebraic curves and surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the maximal number and relative positions of real branches of plane algebraic curves of given order (building on Harnack's result) and analogous questions for algebraic surfaces (e.g., maximal number of sheets for quartic surfaces). Also study the number, form, and position of Poincaré limit cycles for first-order differential equations with rational integral coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for 6th-order plane curves (max 11 branches per Harnack), determine relative embedding possibilities (Hilbert gives configurations he found). For surfaces (4th order in 3-space) the maximum number of sheets is unknown. Use continuous variation of coefficients and methods from algebraic geometry and differential equations to analyze families of curves and Poincaré cycles for equations of the form dy/dx = Y/X with X,Y rational integral of degree n (homogeneous formulation provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of definite forms by squares
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether every definite rational integral form (one nonnegative for all real variable values) can be expressed as a quotient of sums of squares of forms, and whether coefficients for the representing forms can be taken from the same field of rationality as the given form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert has proved that not every definite form is a sum of squares (but affirmative for ternary forms). The question is whether every definite form is representable as (sum_of_squares)/(sum_of_squares) with appropriate forms, possibly with coefficients in the same algebraic realm as the original coefficients. This has implications for geometric constructibility and requires algebraic investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building up of space from congruent polyhedra
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate groups of motions admitting fundamental regions (tilings by congruent regions) in n-dimensional spaces and, in particular, decide whether n-dimensional Euclidean space admits only a finite number of essentially different kinds of motion groups with a fundamental region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare elliptic (finitely many kinds, finite coverings), hyperbolic (infinitely many kinds, Poincaré polygons), and Euclidean cases (finitely many kinds of groups but infinitely many congruent regions needed for complete covering). Use Jordan's theorem on finiteness of finite linear substitution groups, and draw on results by Fricke & Klein, Fedorov, Schoenflies, and Rohn. Generalization to n-dimensions may present difficulties and is the core question.
